UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: almost every upper-limb clinical scenario comes down to a nerve, a vessel, or a bone in the wrong place at the wrong time. A fracture at a predictable site injures a predictable nerve, producing a predictable deformity and sensory loss. Learn the site → nerve → motor loss → sensory loss → deformity chain and most OSCE and written questions fall out of it.
Peripheral Nerve Injuries — The Master Table

Five nerves account for nearly all upper-limb neurology. Learn this grid cold — the rest of the section just expands each row.

Two look-alikes you must separate. Hand of benediction = a high median lesion, seen only when the patient tries to make a fist (index & middle stay extended). Ulnar claw = an ulnar lesion, seen at rest (ring & little finger hyperextend at the MCP, flex at the IP joints). Benediction is active; claw is resting.
The Deformities — Recognise Them on Sight
✋ Wrist drop — Radial nerve
  • All wrist/finger extensors paralysed → wrist and fingers hang flexed
  • Cause: midshaft humeral # (nerve in the spiral groove) or prolonged arm-over-chair compression (“Saturday night palsy”)
  • A high lesion also weakens triceps; a low (posterior interosseous) lesion spares wrist extension but causes finger drop
🙏 Hand of benediction — Median nerve
Benediction: Kencf0618, CC BY-SA 4.0 (posture demonstration). Ape hand: Emily Barrett, CC BY 3.0. Both via Wikimedia Commons.
  • On making a fist, the index & middle fingers cannot flex (lost FDS/FDP + lateral lumbricals) — they stay pointing
  • Chronic: thenar wasting + “ape hand” (thumb pulled into the plane of the palm, lost opposition)
  • High lesion = elbow (supracondylar #); low lesion = wrist (carpal tunnel)
🤚 Ulnar claw — Ulnar nerve
  • Ring & little finger: hyperextended at MCP, flexed at IP (lost medial 2 lumbricals/interossei, unopposed long flexors/extensors)
  • Ulnar paradox: a higher (elbow) lesion gives a less obvious claw — because medial FDP is also paralysed, so the fingertips can’t curl. The claw worsens as a distal lesion or as a proximal one recovers.
  • Froment’s sign: to grip paper the patient flexes FPL (median) to compensate for a weak adductor pollicis
🪽 Winged scapula — Long thoracic nerve
  • Serratus anterior paralysed → medial scapular border lifts off the chest wall, worse on pushing against a wall
  • Also loses the ability to raise the arm above 90° (scapular rotation)
  • Classic cause: axillary node clearance / mastectomy
Benediction vs ulnar claw — the classic mix-up. They look alike (ring & little bent, index & middle straighter), but they are opposite nerves shown at opposite moments. The trick is to ask which fingers are the faulty ones.
🙏 Benediction = MEDIAN
  • Only when making a fist (active)
  • The straight fingers (index + middle) are the faulty ones — median can’t flex them
  • = failure to flex
🤚 Ulnar claw = ULNAR
  • Present at rest (no effort)
  • The bent fingers (ring + little) are the faulty ones — clawed
  • = failure to extend
One-liner: Benediction = can’t make a fist (median). Claw = can’t straighten out (ulnar).
Brachial Plexus Injuries
👶 Erb’s palsy — upper trunk (C5–C6)
  • Mechanism: excessive head–shoulder separation — shoulder dystocia at birth, or a fall onto the shoulder in adults
  • Lost: abductors + external rotators + elbow flexors/supinators
  • Posture: arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated = “waiter’s tip”
  • Roots: C5–C6 (“Erb–six”)
✊ Klumpke’s palsy — lower trunk (C8–T1)
🖼️

Klumpke’s — claw hand ± Horner’s
  • Mechanism: excessive abduction — grabbing something when falling, or arm pulled overhead at birth
  • Lost: all the small muscles of the hand (intrinsics)
  • Posture: claw hand
  • May injure the nearby sympathetic T1 fibres → Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)
Plexus roadmap — “Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer”: Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches. Roots C5–T1; three trunks (upper/middle/lower); each splits into anterior & posterior divisions; three cords (lateral, posterior, medial — named by their relation to the axillary artery); then the five terminal branches (musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, ulnar).

Scaphoid — the fracture you must not miss. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a FOOSH is scaphoid # until proven otherwise. Its blood supply enters distally (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery) and runs retrograde, so a proximal-pole fracture starves the proximal fragment → AVN & non-union. It is often invisible on the initial X-ray — if clinically suspected, immobilise in a thumb spica and re-image (repeat X-ray or MRI) in 10–14 days. Never discharge as “sprain”.
Nerve Compression Syndromes

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome — median nerve at the wrist

🧱 The tunnel
  • Roof = flexor retinaculum; floor/walls = carpal bones
  • Contents = 9 tendons + median nerve (4× FDS, 4× FDP, 1× FPL)
  • The palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel → sensation over the thenar skin is spared in CTS (key discriminator)
🩺 Clinical
  • Paraesthesia of the lateral 3½ fingers, worse at night, shaken out
  • Late: thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction/opposition
  • Tests: Tinel’s (tap) & Phalen’s (flex) reproduce symptoms
  • Causes — “MEDIAN TRAP”: pregnancy, hypothyroid, diabetes, RA, acromegaly, obesity, dialysis
  • Mx: wrist splint → steroid injection → carpal tunnel decompression (divide the retinaculum)
Cubital tunnel — ulnar at the elbow
  • Ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle (the “funny bone”)
  • Numb medial 1½ fingers, weak grip/pinch, clawing
  • Worse with sustained elbow flexion (leaning on the elbow)
Guyon’s canal — ulnar at the wrist
  • Ulnar nerve + artery between pisiform & hook of hamate
  • “Cyclist’s palsy” — handlebar pressure; also ganglia
  • Spares the dorsal ulnar skin (its dorsal branch leaves proximally)
Shoulder — Dislocation & the Rotator Cuff
🎯 Dislocation
  • Anterior (~95%) — arm abducted + externally rotated; risks the axillary nerve (check regimental-badge sensation & deltoid before and after reduction)
  • Posterior — seizures, electrocution, shock; “lightbulb sign” on X-ray
  • Bony Bankart / Hill–Sachs lesions predispose to recurrence
💪 Rotator cuff — “SITS”
  • Supraspinatus — initiates abduction (0–15°); most commonly torn / impinged
  • Infraspinatus — external rotation
  • Teres minor — external rotation
  • Subscapularis — internal rotation
  • Painful arc 60–120° suggests supraspinatus impingement
Vascular Access, the Cubital Fossa & Compartment Syndrome
Cubital fossa — “TAN” (lateral→medial)
  • Tendon of biceps · Arterial (brachial) · Nerve (median)
  • Roof holds the median cubital vein — the standard venepuncture site
  • Borders: pronator teres (medial), brachioradialis (lateral), intercondylar line (superior)
  • Brachial artery here = where the BP cuff auscultates
Arterial access & Allen’s test
  • Radial artery — site for ABGs & arterial lines
  • Allen’s test first: confirm ulnar collateral supply via the palmar arches before cannulating the radial
Forearm compartment syndrome → Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture. Classically follows a supracondylar fracture injuring the brachial artery. Rising compartment pressure → muscle ischaemia → the 6 Ps (Pain out of proportion & on passive stretch, Paraesthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness [late], Paralysis, Perishingly cold). Untreated → fibrosis & a fixed flexion contracture of the wrist & fingers. Treatment is emergency fasciotomy — do not wait for a lost pulse.
The Axilla & Lymphatic Drainage
Axillary nodes
  • Drain the upper limb and ~75% of the breast
  • Grouped in levels I–III relative to pectoralis minor (I below, II behind, III above)
  • First staging site for breast cancer spread → sentinel node biopsy
Cost of axillary clearance
  • Lymphoedema of the arm (disrupted drainage)
  • Intercostobrachial nerve injury → numb medial upper arm
  • Long thoracic nerve → winged scapula
  • Thoracodorsal nerve → weak latissimus dorsi
⭐ Exam Pearls
Site predicts nerve: surgical neck → axillary; midshaft → radial (wrist drop); supracondylar → median + brachial artery; medial epicondyle → ulnar.
Benediction (median, on making a fist) vs claw (ulnar, at rest) — the classic pair to distinguish.
Ulnar paradox: the higher the lesion, the less the claw — because medial FDP is also out.
Erb’s = C5–C6 “waiter’s tip”; Klumpke’s = C8–T1 claw hand ± Horner’s.
Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid # until proven otherwise; normal first X-ray does NOT exclude it — splint & re-image.
CTS spares thenar skin sensation (palmar cutaneous branch bypasses the tunnel) but wastes the thenar muscles.
Always document axillary-nerve function before AND after reducing a dislocated shoulder.
Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis — pain on passive stretch is the earliest sign; fasciotomy before the pulse disappears.
